query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a pack-cementation aluminide coating on equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will form an Al-rich diffusion layer that, upon high-temperature exposure, transforms into a continuous, adherent alumina scale that significantly improves oxygen resistance without compromising the alloy’s intrinsic room-temperature ductility and high-temperature strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Apply a pack-cementation-derived aluminide coating by annealing the alloy at approximately 900 °C for several hours to incorporate aluminum into the near-surface region.
generation.conditions: The improved oxidation resistance will be evaluated under air exposure at 800 °C for up to 5 hours, while ensuring that the loading conditions (strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1) and mechanical performance are maintained.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, continuous, Al-rich diffusion layer that transforms into a protective alumina (Al2O3) scale during oxidation.
generation.mechanism: The aluminide coating promotes the in situ formation of a thermodynamically stable and low-oxygen-permeable alumina scale, which acts as a diffusion barrier to oxygen, thus mitigating the oxidation (and pesting) of the underlying alloy without altering its bulk mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated alloy will exhibit a markedly lower oxidation rate (reduced mass gain) during 5-hour air exposure at 800 °C and will retain its desirable room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr that suffers from inadequate oxygen resistance leading to detrimental oxidation (pesting) when exposed to air at 800 °C.
generation.boundary: Applicable under air exposure at 800 °C for up to 5 hours with the mechanical performance benchmark of 8–16% tensile ductility at room temperature and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1.
generation.uncertainty: The kinetics of alumina scale formation, the uniformity and adhesion of the coating during prolonged high-temperature exposures, and any potential interfacial defects that might affect the mechanical properties remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr samples: one set with the pack-cementation aluminide coating (applied at ~900 °C for several hours) and another set left untreated. Expose both to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. Afterwards, assess the oxide scale via microscopy and X-ray diffraction, quantify mass gain due to oxidation, and perform mechanical tests to confirm retention of room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
measurements: Mass gain per unit area (mg/cm²) to quantify oxidation
Microscopic and XRD analysis to verify formation and adhesion of the alumina scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not show a significant reduction in oxidation (i.e., similar or higher mass gain, poor oxide scale integrity) or if the mechanical properties (ductility and high-temperature strength) are compromised relative to the untreated alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ]. decision.trend: Early work on the same equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr system (PMC5578249) focused on mechanical performance under different casting/HIP conditions and demonstrated excellent high-temperature strength but did not address oxidation. Other refractory HEAs (PMC7513042) have been explored for high-temperature structural applications, including attempts to enhance oxidation resistance via in situ ceramic reinforcement. Nonetheless, a proven route to form a protective oxide scale without compromising mechanical properties remains elusive for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
decision.unsolved: No validated method exists to achieve stable oxidation protection of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr at 800 °C (5 h in air) while conserving its characteristic ductility at room temperature and strength at 1000 °C.
decision.lever: Apply a pack-cementation-derived aluminide coating at ~900 °C for several hours to form a thin, adherent Al-rich diffusion layer that promotes a protective oxide scale (e.g., alumina) without altering the alloy’s bulk composition or mechanical properties
decision.why: Prior HEA oxidation studies (PMC7513042) point to stable oxide scales as key to preventing oxygen ingress under high-temperature exposure. A surface treatment via pack cementation focuses on generating such a scale for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr without bulk alloying changes, which addresses the open challenge that remains after prior work demonstrated only limited pesting resistance in non-equiatomic compositions.
